summary: Defines additional optional DNS resource records for use with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
ILNP is an experimental idea for the Internet that keeps a node's identity separate from the address it currently uses. This RFC adds four new kinds of DNS record so that a resolver can find the identity and the address of another node.

All four records are optional. They must only be present for nodes that support ILNP, because their presence is the signal that tells a node what to expect.

questions: what dns records does ilnp need
what are the ilnp dns record types
what is the difference between nid and l64 records
subtitle: DNS records that separate a node's identity from its location.

tldr.problem: ILNP separates a node's identity from the place it is attached to the network, so software needs a way to look up both in the DNS. The existing DNS record types cannot carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four optional DNS record types. NID holds a node identifier, L32 and L64 hold locators, and LP points at the name where those locators are listed. Every record starts with a 16-bit preference field.
tldr.outcome: The records are optional and must not appear for nodes that do not support ILNP, because their presence is how one node learns that another speaks ILNP.

today: RFC 6742 is an Experimental document produced by the IRTF Routing Research Group, published for examination and evaluation, and it has not been obsoleted. The RFC records that the views in it were considered controversial by the Routing RG, which nevertheless reached a consensus that it should be published, and it notes that IRTF results might not be suitable for deployment.

sections.title: Why ILNP Needs New DNS Records
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) was developed to explore a possible evolutionary direction for the Internet Architecture. It belongs to a class of approaches often called Identifier/Locator Split, where a node keeps an identity that does not change and a locator that changes with the point of attachment. The architecture is described in RFC 6740 and the engineering details in RFC 6741.

The Domain Name System is the standard way that Internet nodes locate information about addresses and other data relating to remote Internet nodes, so ILNP needs to store its identifiers and locators there. This document specifies the syntax and other items required for independent implementations of the new DNS data resource records. The reader is assumed to be familiar with the basics of DNS.

The RFC is part of a wider ILNP document set. Besides the architecture and engineering documents, the set includes new ICMPv6 and ICMPv4 Locator Update messages, a new IPv6 Nonce Destination Option, a new IPv4 Nonce Option and IPv4 Identifier Option, extensions to Address Resolution Protocol for ILNPv4, and optional engineering and deployment functions. Two engineering instances of ILNP are named: ILNPv6, which is based on and backwards compatible with IPv6, and ILNPv4, which is based on and backwards compatible with IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: ILNP keeps a node's identity separate from its network address. This RFC adds the DNS records needed to look both up, so that software on one node can find out how to reach another.

sections.title: The Four New Record Types
sections.content:
Four new record types are defined, with the mnemonics NID, L32, L64 and LP. They are all associated with a fully qualified domain name, which the RFC calls the owner name.

  • The NID record holds Node Identifiers for ILNP-capable nodes. The NodeID is an unsigned 64-bit value that complies with the syntactic rules of IPv6 interface identifiers but has different semantics: it is bound to a specific node rather than to one interface, and it may be used with any interface of that node. The type value is 104.
  • The L32 record holds 32-bit locators for ILNPv4-capable nodes. Its Locator32 field is identical on the wire to the ADDRESS field of an existing DNS A record. The type value is 105.
  • The L64 record holds unsigned 64-bit locators for ILNPv6-capable nodes. Its Locator64 field has the same syntax and semantics as a 64-bit IPv6 routing prefix. The type value is 106.
  • The LP record holds the name of a subnetwork, and that name can then be looked up to find L32 or L64 records. It is, in effect, a Locator Pointer to those records. The type value is 107.

Every record also carries a 16-bit Preference field that says how much the owner name prefers that record over the other records with the same owner name. Lower Preference values are preferred over higher ones. All four types are class independent and have no special time to live requirements.

The records must only be present for nodes that support ILNP. An ILNP-capable node uses the presence of these records in the DNS to learn that a correspondent node is also ILNP-capable. Erroneous records for a node that is not capable would not prevent communication, but they could increase the delay at the start of an IP session.
sections.plainLanguage: Four record types are added: one for a node's identity, two for the addresses it currently uses, and one that points at the place where those addresses are listed. Each record also carries a number that says which of several records to prefer.

sections.title: The NID Record on the Wire
sections.content:
The RDATA of an NID record consists of a 16-bit Preference field and a 64-bit NodeID field. The Preference field is an unsigned 16-bit integer in network byte order that indicates the owner name's relative preference for this NID record among the other NID records associated with that owner name.

In the presentation format used in a DNS configuration file, the Preference field must be written as a 16-bit unsigned decimal integer, and the NodeID must use the same syntax as DNS AAAA records, that is, groups of four hexadecimal digits with each group separated by a colon. The NodeID value must not use the compressed format such as ::, because the NID is a 64-bit field and the compressed form could be confused with a 128-bit IPv6 address.

A given owner name may have zero or more NID records at a given time, and in normal operation a node that supports ILNP will have at least one valid NID record. The examples given in the RFC look like this:

host1.example.com. IN NID 10 0014:4fff:ff20:ee64
host1.example.com. IN NID 20 0015:5fff:ff21:ee65
host2.example.com. IN NID 10 0016:6fff:ff22:ee66
sections.plainLanguage: The NID record holds a 16-bit preference number and a 64-bit identifier. The identifier is written in the same hexadecimal form as an IPv6 interface identifier, but without the shortened form that could be mistaken for a full IPv6 address.

sections.title: The Locator Records L32, L64 and LP
sections.content:
The L32 record holds 32-bit locators for ILNPv4-capable nodes. Its RDATA is a 16-bit Preference field and a 32-bit Locator32 field, which is identical on the wire to the ADDRESS field of an existing DNS A record. In a configuration file the Locator32 uses the same dotted-decimal syntax as an A record.

The L64 record holds unsigned 64-bit locators for ILNPv6-capable nodes. Its RDATA is a 16-bit Preference field and a 64-bit Locator64 field, which has the same syntax and semantics as a 64-bit IPv6 routing prefix. In a configuration file the Locator64 uses the same syntax as an AAAA record, and the compressed display format such as :: must not be used, because the Locator64 is a 64-bit value while an IPv6 address is a 128-bit value.

The LP record holds the name of a subnetwork. Its RDATA is a 16-bit Preference field and a variable-length FQDN field that names the target used to reference L32 and/or L64 records. The FQDN must not have the same value as the owner name of the LP record, and a sender must not use DNS name compression on that field. LP provides one level of indirection inside the DNS when naming a locator value. That is useful for a multihomed site whose multihoming is handled entirely by the site's border routers, and in some mobile network deployment scenarios.

A host that is multihomed normally has several locator values under its owner name, and the Preference field says which of them the owner would rather have used. A name that stands for a subnetwork rather than a host may have an L32 or L64 record as a wild-card entry that applies to the entries under that name.
sections.plainLanguage: The L32 and L64 records hold the addresses a node currently uses, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6. The LP record holds the name of a subnetwork, so a lookup can be pointed at the place where those addresses are listed.

sections.title: Using the Records in a Deployment
sections.content:
Given a domain name, the DNS can be used to discover the set of NID records, the set of L32 records, the set of L64 records and the set of LP records associated with that owner name. One NID record together with one L64 record is the minimum for an ILNPv6 node that is connected to the Internet at the subnetwork with that routing prefix. Two L64 records for the same owner name indicate that the node is multihomed, along with the relative preference a client would use when choosing a locator.

For a node that is part of a mobile network, a query may return an NID record and an LP record, and a further query for the name in the LP record returns the current locator values:

host1.example.com. IN NID 10 0014:4fff:ff20:ee64
host1.example.com. IN LP  10 mobile-net1.example.com.
mobile-net1.example.com. IN L64 2001:0DB8:8140:8000

This lookup process is the forward direction. The Preference fields on all four record types indicate the owner name's preference for one particular record rather than another with the same owner name. A DNS stub resolver querying for one of these record types may not receive all the NID, L32, L64 and LP records in a single response, because a recursive cache may drop additional data records it did not expect, and because resolvers may purge some record sets before others when their time to live values differ. The stub resolver should therefore send follow-up queries for the record types that are missing and wanted.

Nodes likely to be mobile or multihomed normally have very low time to live values for L32 and L64 records, because those values might change frequently. The time to live values for NID and LP records normally are higher, because those values are not normally affected by changes of node location. Existing DNS servers that do not explicitly support the new record types are expected to follow the existing standards for handling unknown DNS records.
sections.plainLanguage: A client looks up a name and gets back the identity and the addresses of that node. It may have to ask a second time for records the server left out, and mobile or multihomed nodes keep their address records short-lived because they change often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the new DNS resource record types do not create any new vulnerabilities in the Domain Name System. The existing mechanisms for DNS security can be used unchanged with these record types, and the RFC says those mechanisms are believed to be widely implemented in currently available DNS servers and clients, with deployment appearing to grow rapidly.

In situations where authentication of DNS data is a concern, the DNS security extensions should be used. If the records are updated dynamically over the network, the secure dynamic DNS update mechanism should be used to secure such transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: The new records do not add any new weakness to DNS. The usual DNS security extensions protect them, including when the records are changed over the network.

fields.name: Preference
fields.desc: 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. Lower values are preferred.

fields.name: NodeID
fields.desc: Unsigned 64-bit value bound to a node, usable with any interface of that node.

viz.caption: The four new DNS record types and their assigned type values

items.title: NID, type 104
items.text: Holds the 64-bit identifier of an ILNP-capable node.

items.title: L32, type 105
items.text: Holds a 32-bit locator for an ILNPv4-capable node, in the same form as an A record.

items.title: L64, type 106
items.text: Holds a 64-bit locator for an ILNPv6-capable node, in the same form as a 64-bit IPv6 routing prefix.

items.title: LP, type 107
items.text: Holds the name of a subnetwork where the L32 and L64 records are found.

data.title: Example DNS records
data.code:
host1.example.com. IN NID 10 0014:4fff:ff20:ee64
host1.example.com. IN L64 10 2001:0DB8:1140:1000
host1.example.com. IN LP  10 mobile-net1.example.com.
mobile-net1.example.com. IN L64 2001:0DB8:8140:8000
